case_name: Carhoun & Sons Enterprises Ltd. v. Canada (Attorney General)
text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Carhoun & Sons Enterprises Ltd. v.
Canada (Attorney General),

2016 BCSC 500

Date: 20160322

Docket:
S133770

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Carhoun & Sons Enterprises Ltd.

Plaintiff

And

The Attorney General of Canada

Defendant

Corrected Judgment: The text of the judgment was corrected at page 1
where changes were made on April 1, 2016

Before: The Honourable Chief Justice Hinkson

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiff:

J.D.
Shields and A. Wade

Counsel for the Defendant:

E.G.
McDonald and R.J. Danay

Place and Date of Hearing:

Vancouver,
B.C.

February
11, 2016

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver,
B.C.

March
22, 2016

Introduction

[
1
]

The plaintiff Carhoun & Sons Enterprises
Ltd. ("Carhoun") has framed its action against the Attorney General
of Canada ("Canada") respecting the manner in which Canada
adjudicated Carhoun's applications for authorization to infill and develop potential
fish habitat areas under
s. 35(2)
of the
Fisheries Act
, R.S.C.
1985, c. F-14 [
Act
] in both negligence and misfeasance.  Authorization
under s. 35(2) of the
Act
, at the relevant times, provided for an
exception from any possible liability flowing from resulting harmful
alteration, disruption, or destruction of fish habitat.

[
2
]

Although the exception sought by the plaintiff
was ultimately issued with conditions, Carhoun asserts that it was issued so
late that it suffered foreseeable economic loss and claims damages for that
loss.

[
3
]

Canada contends that it owes no duty of care in
negligence to applicants pursuant to
s. 35(2)
of the
Act
. Canada
sought an order that Carhoun’s pleadings failed to establish a cause of action
in misfeasance and sought to dismiss Carhoun’s notice of civil claim. On June
18, 2014, that application was dismissed by Mr. Justice Wong in reasons
for judgment indexed at
2014 BCSC 1295
. Canada obtained leave to appeal the
dismissal of its application from a Justice of the Court of Appeal sitting in chambers,
and in the alternative, sought further and better particulars of Carhoun’s
claim.

[
4
]

On April 21, 2015, Madam Justice Garson for a
unanimous Court dismissed Canada’s appeal to strike the pleadings in both negligence
and misfeasance, in reasons for judgment indexed at
Carhoun & Sons
Enterprises Ltd. v. Canada (Attorney General)
,
2015 BCCA 163
. She held at paras. 128
– 129 with respect to Canada’s alleged duty of care to Carhoun that it was not
plain and obvious that Carhoun’s claim would fail because it was not clear that
Canada did not owe a duty of care to Carhoun.

[
5
]

With respect to the alleged misfeasance in
public office claim, Garson J.A. held that the claim could be amended to
provide the necessary material facts and to meet the test in
Odahvji Estate
v. Woodhouse
,
2003 SCC 69
.

[
6
]

Garson J.A. granted liberty to Carhoun to amend
its pleading in misfeasance to make out its claim. Garson J.A. also allowed
Canada’s appeal to the extent of ordering Carhoun to respond to some of
Canada’s demand for particulars.

[
7
]

The trial of this action is now set for up to 60
days, to commence on January 30, 2017.

Orders Sought

[
8
]

Carhoun applied for an order to amend its notice
of civil claim. Its application was opposed by Canada, and I dismissed the
application on February 11, 2016, on the basis that the proposed amendments
went far beyond what was contemplated by the Court of Appeal.

[
9
]

Canada now seeks an order for security for
costs. Its application is opposed by Carhoun. If its application is granted,
Canada seeks a stay of the action until any ordered security is paid.

Legal Framework

[
10
]

Section 236
of the
Business Corporations Act,

S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, affords the Court the discretion to order security for
costs where a corporation is the plaintiff in a legal proceeding and it appears
that the corporation will be unable to pay the costs of the defendant if the
defendant is successful. The discretion is to be exercised in light of all the
relevant circumstances.

[
11
]

The purpose of an order for security for costs
is to protect a defendant from the likelihood that, in the event of its
success, it will be unable to recover its costs from the plaintiff.

[
12
]

For important policy reasons, the test to be
met to obtain an order for security of costs against a corporate plaintiff is
far less onerous than that which applies to a natural person. In
Apex Mountain Resort Ltd. v. British Columbia
,
[1998]
B.C.J. No. 1918
, Bauman J., as he then was, considered an application by
the defendant for security for costs. He noted two decisions from the Court of
Appeal that he described as instructive:
Fat Mel's Restaurant Ltd. v.
Canadian Northern Shield Insurance Co.
(1993),
1993 CanLII 1669 (BC CA)
, 76 B.C.L.R. (2d) 231 and
Kropp
v. Swaneset Bay Golf Courts Ltd
.,
1997 CanLII 4037 (BC CA)
, [1997] 4 W.W.R. 306.

[
13
]

At para. 20, Bauman J. cited the principle
from
Fat Mel’s
that security for costs should generally be ordered where
it has been shown that the corporation will be unable to pay costs should its
claim fail, with some exceptions. He then explained the limitations of the
guidance provided by the general principle:

[21]      While
helpful, that statement offers no guidance on the circumstances in which the
court should decline to do that which is "generally ordered." I say
this because it is clear that by simply demonstrating that a plaintiff will be
unable to pay costs should the claim fail and that there is an arguable
defence, a defendant will not invariably take his or her order. There remains a
residual discretion. How ought the judge to approach its exercise?

[
14
]

Citing
Kropp
, Bauman J. went on to
conclude that the Court should apply the factors set out in
Keary
Developments Ltd. v. Tarmac Construction Ltd. and another
,
[1995] 3 All
E.R. 534 (Eng. C.A.) [
Keary
]

to determine whether to exercise its
discretion to order security for costs.

[
15
]

The seven factors set out in
Keary
can be
summarized as follows:

a)

the Court’s complete discretion whether to order security;

b)

the possibility or probability that the plaintiff will be deterred
from pursuing its claim;

c)

the balance of injustices between the use of security to stifle the
plaintiff’s legitimate claim and the use of impecuniosity as a means of putting
unfair pressure on the defendant. As part of this balancing exercise, the Court
considers whether it is the defendant's conduct that rendered the
corporate plaintiff impecunious:
Integrated Contractors
Ltd. v. Leduc Development Ltd.
,
2009 BCSC 965
at para.
14
;

d)

a consideration of the merits of the action, which the Court should
not go into in detail unless success or failure appears obvious;

e)

the amount of security to be ordered, which can be up to the full
amount claimed as long as it is more than nominal;

f)

if the Court refuses to order security because
it would unfairly stifle a valid claim, it must be satisfied that it is probable
that the claim would be stifled. The Court should consider both whether the
plaintiff can provide security out of its own resources and whether it can
raise the security from its directors, shareholders, financial backers,
lenders, or other interested persons; and

g)

the lateness of the application for security, especially where the
plaintiff has been lulled into a false sense of safety and has therefore been
prejudiced by the delay:
Honda Canada Inc. v. Tonka Motorcycle Sales
Ltd.
(1986),
1986 CanLII 761 (BC CA)
, 7 B.C.L.R. (2d) 124 at para.
8
(C.A.).

[
16
]

Procedurally, once a defendant has established a

prima facie
case that the corporate plaintiff may be unable to pay
costs, the onus then shifts to the corporation to show that it does in fact
have sufficient exigible assets to pay costs if it is unsuccessful in the
action.

[
17
]

In terms of the quantum of security for costs that is ultimately
ordered, the Court may consider whether the defendant has claimed the maximum
amount allowable in its estimated costs and whether the cost of trial could be
avoided by early settlement.

Discussion

[
18
]

The facts underlying this action are
conveniently summarized by Canada in  its notice of application:

1.         Karel
and Philip Carhoun are brothers who run a real estate development business.
They are the directors of three companies incorporated under the laws of
British Columbia: Carhoun Holdings Ltd., which, in turn, owns all of the shares
of Carhoun and Sons Enterprises Ltd. (i.e. the Plaintiff in these
proceedings) and Bullet Enterprises Ltd. (collectively, the “Carhoun
companies”).

2.         Along
with an alter ego trust in favour of their mother, Margaret Carhoun, Karel and
Philip Carhoun own all of the shares of Carhoun Holdings.

3.         In
1986, the Plaintiff purchased three adjoining lots on Fletcher Street in
Mission, upon which an office space was located (“Fletcher property”). On
September 1, 2005, the Plaintiff borrowed $1.8 million from JNJJ Enterprises
Ltd. This loan was secured by,
inter alia,
a mortgage on the Fletcher
property. The mortgage provided for monthly payments to be made by the
Plaintiff to JNJJ Enterprises Ltd on the first of every month.

4.         On
November 6, 2007, the Plaintiff borrowed $400,000 from HSBC Bank Canada. The
loan was secured by a mortgage over one of the lots on the Fletcher property.

5.         Between
1988 and 2006, the Plaintiff purchased five adjoining lots of land in Mission
for the purposes of development. A sixth adjoining lot, which was also intended
for development, was purchased by Philip Carhoun’s spouse, Susan Carhoun in
2009 (collectively, the “Mission Properties”).

6.         In
April of 2007, the Plaintiff borrowed $3,750,000 from Coast Capital Savings
Credit Union (“Coast Capital”). This loan was secured by,
inter alia,
a
mortgage on the Mission Properties.

7.         Bullet
Enterprises Ltd. was incorporated in 1994. In 2001 it purchased a commercial
property on Sumas Way in Abbotsford (“Sumas Way property”). Between 2006 and
2008, it built a motel and three buildings for restaurants that became
commercial tenants on the property. It also owned its own office space in
Vancouver.

8.         In
order to develop the Sumas Way property and to purchase office space in
Vancouver, in 2006 Bullet Enterprises Ltd. borrowed approximately $11 million
from Canadian Western Bank. The term of the loan was 1 year and was secured by,

inter alia,
a mortgage on the property and an assignment of rents. This
loan was extended in 2007, 2008 and 2009.

9.         On
April 24, 2008, the Plaintiff borrowed an additional $170,000 from JNJJ
Enterprises Ltd. pursuant to its existing mortgage agreement. It borrowed a
further $100,000 under the mortgage on November 5, 2008 and a further $150,000
on November 18, 2008. The Plaintiff then defaulted on its mortgage by failing
to make required monthly payments beginning on December 1, 2009 and continuing
through May 1, 2010. After December 1, 2011, the Plaintiff made no further
payments to JNJJ Enterprises Ltd.

10.       Despite
having repeatedly defaulted on its mortgage payments beginning in 2009, the
Plaintiff borrowed a further $100,000 from JNJJ Enterprises Ltd. on December 6,
2011. The Plaintiff also failed to pay the property taxes that were owing on
the Fletcher property in both 2012 and 2013. These payments (which totalled
more than $100,000) were made by JNJJ Enterprises Inc. and in the Plaintiffs
stead so as to avoid foreclosure.

11.       As
early as 2009, Bullet Enterprises Ltd. also began having financial problems. In
both 2009 and 2010, it failed to pay its property taxes on the Sumas Way
property and by April 30, 2010 it had failed to make several loan payments to
Canadian Western Bank. By September 22, 2010, Canadian Western Bank indicated
that, as a result, it would act on its assignment of rents and, if necessary,
foreclose on the Sumas Way property.

12.       In
order to avoid foreclosure by Canadian Western Bank, in October and November of
2010, Bullet Enterprises (along with the Plaintiff, Carhoun Holdings, Philip
and Karel Carhoun and their respective spouses), borrowed $15,400,000 from Imor
Capital Corp. (“Imor Capital”). This loan was secured by debentures that
granted charges over the Sumas Way Property and the Mission Properties

13.       On
October 6, 2011, Bullet Enterprises Ltd. borrowed $375,000 from Courbet
Properties Ltd. secured by a mortgage over its office space in Vancouver.

14.       By 2012,
the Carhoun companies had collectively amassed approximately $21,125,000 in
debt and had defaulted on several of these loans. These defaults precipitated
numerous foreclosure proceedings, which included (but were not limited to):

a.

Proceedings initiated by Imor Capital (S-S-123055 and H-120498),
which resulted in the appointment of a receiver and the sale of the Sumas Way
property for $12,050,000.

b.

Proceedings initiated by Coast Capital (H-121061) in which an
order of conduct of sale in respect of the Mission Properties was granted.

c.

Proceedings initiated by Courbet Properties Ltd. (H-151327),
which resulted in an order of conduct of sale in respect of Bullet Enterprise’s
office space.

d.

Proceedings initiated by HSBC Bank Canada (H-130132), which
resulted in the court approved sale of one lot on the Fletcher property for
$210,000 (which is less than the $213,190.73 owed to HSBC Bank of Canada as of
December 21, 2012).

e.

Proceedings initiated by JNJJ Enterprises Ltd. (VLC-S-S-138910),
which resulted in sale of two other lots on the Fletcher property for
$1,450,000 (which is less than the $2,592,268.64 that was owing to JNJJ
Enterprises Ltd as of November 1, 2013).

15.       As of
January 7, 2016, Imor Capital continues to hold a registered PPSA security
agreement that covers “all present and after acquired personal property and an
uncrystallized floating charge on land” in which the Carhoun companies are
named as debtors.

16.       As of
January 8, 2016, none of the Carhoun companies own any real estate.

…

18.       The Plaintiff filed a Notice of
Civil Claim on May 24, 2013 (the “Claim”). The Plaintiff alleges that the
Defendant was negligent and committed the tort of misfeasance in public office
by taking too long to grant the Plaintiff an authorization under
s. 35(2)

of the
Fisheries Act,
R.S.C. 1985, c. F-14 to destroy fish habitat.
The Plaintiff sought this authorization on September 9, 2009 in furtherance of
a proposed development on the Mission Properties. The authorization was granted
on May 29, 2012.

[
19
]

Mr. Karel Carhoun deposed in his affidavit
sworn February 10, 2016 that annual reports were filed on February 7, 2016 for
Carhoun & Sons Enterprises Ltd. for February 14, 2015, and for Carhoun
Holdings Ltd. for December 31, 2015.

[
20
]

Of the
Keary
factors, some favour Canada,
but others favour the plaintiff. I will discuss each in turn below.

a)         The Court’s complete discretion

[
21
]

This first factor needs no explanation.

b)        The possibility
that the plaintiff will be deterred from pursuing its claim

[
22
]

As I will explain below, I am satisfied that the
plaintiff’s claim will be stifled if it is ordered to pay security for costs
that it cannot reasonably be expected to fund.

c)         Balancing
the injustice arising of stifling a legitimate claim against the use of
impecuniosity as a means of putting unfair pressure on a defendant

[
23
]

The plaintiff concedes that it will be unable to
pay an award of costs should it be unsuccessful at the trial of this action.
This fact must be weighed against the reality, as I will explain below, that the
plaintiff’s claim will be stifled if it is ordered to pay security for costs
that it cannot reasonably be expected to fund.

[
24
]

This factor also includes consideration of
whether the defendant’s conduct rendered the plaintiff impecunious. The
plaintiff’s claim, if proven, is that Canada is responsible for its
impecuniosity because it failed to fairly consider the plaintiff’s application
for an exception under the
Act

within a reasonable time, thus rendering
it incapable of pursuing its planned development by the time that the qualified
exemption was granted.

[
25
]

The cause of a party’s impecuniosity was
considered by Mr. Justice Ehrcke in
Beasse et al v. Holness et al
,

2006 BCSC 1265
[
Beasse
]. At para. 24 of his reasons for
judgment Ehrcke J. commented:

[24]      In
almost every action it will be possible for the plaintiffs to assert that they
have suffered a loss because of the actions of the defendants; that is what
lawsuits are typically all about. So in this sense, plaintiffs who claim to be
impecunious will almost always be able to say that their impecuniosity is
linked to the conduct of the defendants and to the very subject matter of the
lawsuit. In assessing this as a factor, therefore, consideration must be given
to how remote the alleged connection is.

[
26
]

The defendants contend that by September of 2009
when the plaintiff submitted its application for an exemption, both the
plaintiff and its associated company Bullet Enterprises Ltd. were indebted for
millions of dollars and beginning to default on their payments on those
obligations. Canada eschews the plaintiff’s contention that had it obtained its
exemption from Canada, it would have avoided the foreclosure applications that
it was ultimately unable to overcome.

[
27
]

I am unable to resolve the issue at this stage,
but I am far from satisfied that the plaintiff’s position on this point is not meritorious.

d)        The merits of the claim and the defence

[
28
]

I accept Canada’s submission that it has raised
a plausible defence to the plaintiff’s claim.

[
29
]

While not providing a ringing endorsement of the
plaintiff’s claim in negligence, Garson J.A. found at paras. 128 – 129 in
2015
BCCA 163
that:

[128]    In my opinion, it is not plain and
obvious that Canada did not owe a duty of [c]are to Carhoun.

[129]    Since a
duty of care cannot be ruled out at this stage of the proceedings, it is not
plain and obvious that Carhoun's claim would fail.

[
30
]

Similarly, with respect to the plaintiff’s claim
for misfeasance in public office, Garson J.A. found at paras. 131 – 134 of
the same reasons that:

[131]    As discussed, Carhoun pleads at para. 23
of its Notice of Civil Claim that "the DFO displayed a clear bias and
predetermination against the Plaintiff's proposed development and the
Authorization sought by the Plaintiff". Carhoun pleads that rather than
assessing the application on its own merits, it relied on earlier erroneous and
unlawful determinations rejecting the application. Carhoun says such conduct
amounts to bad faith and misfeasance, which led to the unreasonable delay and
the consequent economic damages.

[132]    Carhoun does not identify a
specific public officer or allege that an officer "specifically intended
to injure a person or class of persons":
Odhavji
at paras. 21-22.
Canada argues that the failure to identify such material facts means the claim
should be struck, and cites
Barbour v. UBC
,
2006 BCSC 1897
at para.
45
,
in support of this proposition.

[133]    However, claims should not be
struck out under s. 9-5(1)(a) if the statement as it stands, or as it may
be amended, discloses a cause of action: see
Minnes v. Minnes
(1962),
1962 CanLII 350 (BC CA)
, 39
W.W.R. 112 (B.C.C.A.), cited with approval in Hunt.

[134]    In my
opinion, the misfeasance claim could be amended to provide all necessary material
facts and to meet the test in
Odhavji
. I would grant liberty to Carhoun
to amend the pleadings so it can plead the essential ingredients for a claim in
misfeasance in public office.

[
31
]

I am therefore not satisfied that the claim
advanced by the plaintiff is obviously doomed to fail.

e)         More than nominal security for costs

[
32
]

Canada estimates that its costs and
disbursements, including the attendance of two counsel and the cost of daily
court reporting services, if calculated on Scale B, will be some $372,656.45.
For the purposes of its application for security for costs, Canada is content
to reduce this figure to $306,191.45 to exclude the anticipated cost of the
daily court reporting services. I regard this figure as a reasonable estimate
of Canada’s costs if this case proceeds to trial for the entire estimated 60
days.

[
33
]

The amount sought for security for costs in
Apex
Mountain Resort
was between $390,000 and $540,000. Bauman J. ordered security
for costs of $100,000. In reaching this figure, Bauman J. was clearly
influenced by the fact that the plaintiff had enjoyed some success in raising
funding by entering into agreements with a group of lenders for interim bridge
financing in the amount of $925,000.

[
34
]

In subsequent reasons for judgment in the same
case, reported at
[1999] B.C.J. No. 3288
, prior to the entry of his order,
Bauman J. reconsidered his order for security for costs in the amount of
$100,000. At paras. 4 – 6, Bauman J. held:

[4]        Based on the material before me
at this time, I have concluded that it is probable that the claim will be
stifled if the current order for security remains in place. I quote principles
2 and 3 from the
Keary
decision,
(1995) 3 All E.R. 534
and in my
quotation I delete references to the cases cited there.

2. The possibility or probability that the
plaintiff company will be deterred from pursuing its claim by an order for
security is not, without more, a sufficient reason for not ordering security.
By making the exercise of discretion under section 726(1) conditional on it being
shown that the company is one likely to be unable to pay costs awarded against
it, parliament must have envisaged that the order might be made in respect of a
plaintiff company that would find difficulty in providing security.

3. The court must carry out a balancing
exercise. On the one hand, it must weigh the injustice to the plaintiff if
prevented from pursuing a proper claim by an order for security. Against that,
it must weigh the injustice to the defendant if no security is ordered and at
the trial the plaintiff's claim fails and the defendant finds himself unable to
recover from the plaintiff the costs which have been incurred by him in his
defence of the claim. The court will properly be concerned not to allow the
power to order security to be used as an instrument of oppression, such as by
stifling a genuine claim by an indigent company against a more prosperous
company, particularly when the failure to meet that claim might in itself have
been a material cause of the plaintiff's impecuniosity. But it will also be
concerned not to be so reluctant to order security that it becomes a weapon
whereby the impecunious company can use its inability to pay costs as a means
of putting unfair pressure on the more prosperous company.

[5]        I am
engaged then in a balancing exercise, weighing the injustice to the plaintiff
if it is prevented from pursuing a valid claim and the prejudice to the Crown
if it prevails and it cannot collect its costs.

[6]        In all the circumstances of this
claim and these parties, I have concluded that this is definitely not a case of
an impecunious plaintiff using its inability to pay costs as a means of putting
unfair pressure on the more prosperous defendant. In light of the new evidence,
I have concluded that a judicial exercise of my discretion requires that
security be reduced to the sum of $10,000.

[
35
]

Given the magnitude of the costs sought in the
case, I am not satisfied that the figure of $10,000 fixed by Bauman J. is other
than “nominal” in this case, as that term is used in
Keary.

f)          Other sources of funding for the plaintiff

[
36
]

In
Kropp

the Court held at para.
22

that:

To succeed in showing that an order for
security would stifle the action the plaintiff must do more than show that it
has no assets:
see Paul v. General Magnaplate Corp.
(1995),
1995 CanLII 7259 (ON SC)
, 27 O.R. (3d)
314 (Gen.Div.). The defendants have already made out a
prima facie
case
that the corporate plaintiff has insufficient assets to pay costs if
unsuccessful. Mr. Kropp's affidavit does not really add to that position
and establish that the corporate plaintiff is impecunious, in the sense of
lacking
any means of raising money for security
. I think the law requires him to do
so. As Megarry, V.C., said in
Pearson
, supra, at 535, the purpose of the
provision is to protect "the community against litigious abuses by
artificial persons manipulated by natural persons."

[Emphasis added.]

[
37
]

Canada contends that the application of this
aspect of
Kropp
requires the plaintiff to provide thorough and
substantiated evidence including a full accounting of all of its principals’
and other backers’ finances, referring to
Kropp
at

para.
22
;

Deepak Suri Ltd.

v
.
Urban
Choice Market Ltd.
,
2013 BCSC 2460
at para.
39-40
;

Citizens
for Foreign Aid Reform Inc.

v
.
Canadian Jewish Congress
,

1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J. No. 2160 (S.C.) at para.
22
;

Beasse
at para.
26
;

Apex Mountain Resort
at paras. 46–47.
None of these authorities require such extensive evidence, and I do not agree
that such evidence is required. In each case where the financial wherewithal of
a corporate entity is in issue, it will be for the Court hearing the application
to consider the adequacy of the evidence adduced by the corporate entity. More
evidence will be required in some cases than in others.

[
38
]

In his affidavit sworn February 3, 2016, Mr. Karel
Carhoun deposed that he is unable to borrow any money from friends or family in
order to post security for costs, that he owns no real estate which he could
potentially pledge as collateral and that he lives rent-free at a friend’s
apartment. He also deposed in that affidavit that he owns no motor vehicle or
any assets of significance, and that he is unemployed.

[
39
]

In this case, Canada argued before me that there
was an absence of evidence relating to direct evidence from Mr. Philip
Carhoun as to his ability or that of his wife Susan to raise funds for the
litigation. From the material produced by Canada, it appears that Ms. Susan
Carhoun has worked as a realtor and been involved in the sale or purchase of
some six homes.

[
40
]

In order to avoid the difficulty that Bauman J.
was forced to contend with in
Apex Mountain Resort
due to incomplete
information, I gave the plaintiff two weeks to provide further affidavit
information from Mr. Philip Carhoun, and Canada one week to file any
further submissions that it wished me to consider in light of any further
affidavit material from him.

[
41
]

Since hearing the oral submissions in this case,
I have not been provided with any affidavit material from Mr. Philip
Carhoun, but instead have been given a fifth affidavit from Mr. Karel Carhoun.
In his fifth affidavit, Mr. Karel Carhoun deposed in part that:

2.         Philip Carhoun is a Director of
Carhoun Holdings Ltd., Carhoun & Sons Enterprises Ltd. and Bullet
Enterprises Ltd. (the “Carhoun companies”).

3.         Philip Carhoun is also my
brother.

4.         The financial difficulties which
have transpired since April 2012 have caused a considerable deterioration in
the relationship between my brother and me, on both a personal and business
level.

5.         At this time, Philip Carhoun is
not willing to provide an affidavit to the court in respect of this legal
action. He has not responded to email messages since the last court appearance
on February 11, 2016.

6.         To the best of my knowledge, my
brother is employed in the construction industry as a labourer on an hourly
wage.

7.         To the best of my knowledge, my
brother’s wife, Susan Carhoun works as a realtor.

8.         To
the best of my knowledge, my brother and his wife are living in a rented
townhouse. They do not own any property.

[
42
]

This affidavit also responds in part to Canada’s
position that Ms. Susan Carhoun has earned income as a realtor from the
sale or purchase of properties. It calculates the gross commissions that Ms. Susan
Carhoun would have received from these sales based on the information contained
in the listing summaries for five of the six properties at approximately
$54,092, and disputes Canada’s assertion that the sixth property has been sold,
or that Ms. Susan Carhoun is the listing agent for the property.

[
43
]

Canada argues that the information in this
further affidavit fails to show that the order it seeks for security for costs
will unfairly stifle the plaintiff’s claim, as it “contains no tax returns, no
bank statements, no summaries of investments or indeed any documentation that
would substantiate the finances of” the Carhoun brothers “or other potential
financial backers”. In the result, Canada asks that I draw an adverse inference
from what has not been provided.

[
44
]

Canada also argues that Mr. Karel Carhoun’s
most recent affidavit offers no indication as to why Ms. Susan Carhoun has
not sworn an affidavit in these proceedings. However, I accept that the
strained relations between the Carhoun brothers extend to Ms. Susan
Carhoun as well.

[
45
]

While the absence of an affidavit from Phillip or
Susan Carhoun is of concern to me, its absence does not leave me with a
complete lack of information about the financial circumstances of either, and I
decline to draw the adverse inference suggested by Canada.

[
46
]

In his affidavit sworn February 10, 2016, Mr. Karel
Carhoun swore that his parents were not prepared to lend any further monies to
the plaintiff. I reject Canada’s submission that the plaintiff’s principals are
capable of raising funds to employ in posting security for costs. The fact that
they were able to do so in the past is no indication that their ability to do
so is endless. I find, on the evidence before me, that the plaintiff’s
principals have exhausted their borrowing power.

[
47
]

On the evidence before me, I am satisfied that
the Carhoun brothers and Ms. Susan Carhoun are in no position to provide
security for costs, and that the plaintiff therefore cannot post security for
costs in any amount.

g)        The Lateness of the Application

[
48
]

I find that this factor weighs heavily in the
plaintiff’s favour.

[
49
]

To date, the plaintiff has produced some 2,800
documents and the defendant has collected over 5,000 potentially relevant
documents. The plaintiff has completed its examination for discovery of the
defendant’s representative of three and a half days and the defendant
anticipates requiring a similar period of time to complete its examination for
discovery of the plaintiff. Further, on January 28, 2014, the plaintiff served
an extensive 342-page notice to admit facts and documents on the defendant.

[
50
]

As mentioned above, the plaintiff’s claim was
filed on May 24, 2013, and much has now been done in terms of trial
preparation. Canada’s application for security for costs was not filed until
January 27
th
of this year. Canada offers two explanations for the lateness
of the application: its focus on seeking clarity of the case it was to meet;
and the fact that the plaintiff’s estimate of the length of time needed for
trial doubled in September 2015.

[
51
]

I am not persuaded that either explanation is sufficient
to change the balance of this factor. The magnitude and nature of the
plaintiff’s claim has not changed since it was filed. While the notice of civil
claim originally left and still leaves a great deal to be desired, it does not
in my view justify Canada’s delay of almost three years before seeking security
for costs. The original estimate of 25 days for the trial of the matter has now
more than doubled, but even the original estimate raised the likelihood of
significant costs and disbursements.

Conclusion

[
52
]

While I accept as reasonable Canada’s estimate
of its costs if this case proceeds to trial for the entire estimated 60 days, I
decline to order that the plaintiff post security for the defendant’s
anticipated costs at this stage of the proceedings. While the plaintiff’s evidence
might have been better, as I have stated above, I am satisfied on the evidence
before me that the plaintiff’s principals have exhausted their borrowing power,
and that the plaintiff cannot post security for costs.

[
53
]

The plaintiff’s claim is that Canada is
responsible for its impecuniosity because it failed to fairly consider the
plaintiff’s application for an exception under the
Act
within a
reasonable time, thus rendering it incapable of pursuing its planned
development by the time that the qualified exemption was granted. I have found
that this claim is not obviously without merit. If the plaintiff’s claim can be
made out, any order for security for costs would enable Canada to avoid facing
the claim on its merits.

[
54
]

I find further that Canada has delayed
unreasonably in bringing its application for security for costs, and obliged
the plaintiff to address a number of issues that might have been avoided by an
earlier application. To require that the plaintiff now post security for costs
that would effectively stifle its claim would, in my view, strike an inequitable
balance between the use of impecuniosity as a means of putting unfair pressure
on Canada and the injustice arising from stifling a legitimate claim.

[
55
]

As I have indicated above, an order for security
in an amount representing a small portion of Canada’s estimate of its costs if
this case proceeds to trial for the entire estimated 60 days would amount to no
more than a “nominal” amount as that term is used in
Keary
, and is thus inappropriate.

[
56
]

Canada’s application for security for costs is
therefore dismissed.
